title: AI Development Timeline
question: How should a history of attention to AI be read alongside technical milestones?
scope: The red curve measures mentions in books, not capability; winter bands denote historical intervals, not isolated hardware causes.

steps.title: Locate the early approaches
steps.description: Turing, the Dartmouth workshop, the perceptron, and ELIZA appear as dated callouts. These approaches overlapped rather than replacing one another on a fixed schedule.

steps.title: Separate attention from capability
steps.description: The red curve rises and falls through shaded winter intervals. Its height counts publication mentions, so a peak cannot be read as a measured level of intelligence.

steps.title: Read advances as systems combinations
steps.description: Deep Blue and GPT-3 mark later milestones. Their dates locate developments, while the surrounding chapter explains how data, algorithms, and machines jointly changed the feasible systems.

title: AlexNet Architecture
question: How did AlexNet map one network onto two GPUs?
scope: Historical partitioned architecture; schematic arrows are dependencies, not a measured communication schedule.

steps.title: Partition the convolutional work
steps.description: The green blocks form two parallel streams. Each holds part of the network rather than representing two independent models.

steps.title: Exchange only at selected connections
steps.description: Dashed cross-stream connections mark dependencies between the partitions. The historical design limited exchanges because the inter-GPU link was itself a constraint.

steps.title: Converge on classification
steps.description: After the convolution and pooling stages, the fully connected layers combine features into 1,000 outputs. The partition is a model–machine design choice, not simply a larger batch.

title: The D·A·M Axis Triad
question: Where can a relaxed bottleneck reappear in an ML system?
scope: A diagnostic taxonomy, not three independent optimization scores.

steps.title: Diagnose missing information
steps.description: The Data vertex directs attention to coverage, labels, and distributions. Faster machines cannot supply examples that were never collected.

steps.title: Diagnose representation and execution
steps.description: Algorithm asks whether the model can represent the pattern; Machine asks whether execution fits latency, memory, and throughput requirements.

steps.title: Remeasure after an intervention
steps.description: Double-headed edges show coupled requirements. More model capacity can expose memory limits, and faster compute can expose an input bottleneck.

title: The D·A·M Intersection Landscape
question: Which engineering questions belong at the intersections of Data, Algorithm, and Machine?
scope: The overlaps organize joint design questions; their drawn areas are not quantitative proportions.

steps.title: Distinguish the three axes
steps.description: Storage and quality belong to Data, model mathematics to Algorithm, and silicon and memory to Machine. These labels identify kinds of evidence to investigate.

steps.title: Resolve pairwise questions
steps.description: Data–Algorithm asks what to learn from; Data–Machine asks how to move information; Algorithm–Machine asks how to execute efficiently. Each requires choices on both axes.

steps.title: Integrate the constraints
steps.description: The center names ML systems engineering because a useful deployment must satisfy all three axes together. Improving one axis alone does not establish end-to-end success.

title: Algorithmic Efficiency Trajectory
question: What does algorithmic efficiency measure when hardware speed is held out?
scope: Measured compute to reach AlexNet-level ImageNet accuracy; the fitted trend is descriptive rather than a forecast.

steps.title: Fix the quality target
steps.description: AlexNet provides the reference compute required to reach its accuracy. A factor above one means less training compute for this same target, not faster hardware.

steps.title: Keep the exception visible
steps.description: VGG-11 falls below the AlexNet reference despite being later. Publication date alone does not guarantee efficiency at a fixed accuracy.

steps.title: Read progress without treating the fit as law
steps.description: Later architectures reach the target with much less compute, while individual points vary around the dashed fit. The fit summarizes these measurements rather than predicting every future model.

title: The Era of Scale
question: What does a rising training-compute estimate imply about systems requirements?
scope: Third-party final-training compute estimates for selected notable models; log-scale evidence, not inference cost or a capability score.

steps.title: Read logarithmic orders of magnitude
steps.description: AlexNet and early points occupy the lower part of the FLOPs axis. Equal vertical distances represent multiplicative differences, not equal added operations.

steps.title: Distinguish estimates from requirements
steps.description: Later red points exceed the plotted 10²²-FLOP category threshold. They show selected training-run estimates, not a universal minimum for useful ML.

steps.title: Use the trend to motivate infrastructure
steps.description: The fitted line summarizes rapid growth across the plotted runs. It does not establish a hardware growth law or predict the cost of a particular future training job.

title: ML System Lifecycle
question: Why do evaluation failure and production degradation lead to different rework?
scope: A lifecycle schematic; return arrows express decisions rather than fixed iteration durations.

steps.title: Validate before deployment
steps.description: Collection and preparation feed model training, followed by evaluation. Only a model meeting requirements advances along the labeled deployment path.

steps.title: Revise a failed candidate
steps.description: The Needs Improvement arrow returns from evaluation to preparation. Evidence at this gate can require changing data preparation before training again.

steps.title: Use production evidence to revisit the data
steps.description: Monitoring observes deployed behavior. The longer Performance Degrades return reaches data collection because production problems can require new evidence rather than just another training run.

title: The Efficiency Frontier
question: Which models offer more accuracy for a given arithmetic budget?
scope: Published representative model reports; the dashed frontier is illustrative, not a controlled benchmark.

steps.title: Low arithmetic cost
steps.description: MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-B0 occupy the low-compute side. Their different accuracies show why arithmetic cost alone does not identify a model.

steps.title: Accuracy at moderate cost
steps.description: Compare ResNet-50, Inception-v3, Swin-T, and ConvNeXt-T. A model above and left of another offers a more favorable plotted accuracy–compute pair.

steps.title: An expensive point need not dominate
steps.description: ViT-B/16 lies below the illustrative frontier despite its greater reported arithmetic cost. Model variant, image resolution, and training recipe remain part of this comparison.

title: Multilayer Perceptron Architecture
question: How does one densely connected neuron become a matrix operation?
scope: The drawn network is schematic; the MNIST dimensions in the caption describe a larger example.

steps.title: Every input contributes
steps.description: The green hidden neuron receives an edge from every input neuron. Each edge carries a learned weight.

steps.title: One column produces one activation
steps.description: The highlighted weight-matrix column collects those incoming weights. Multiplying the input vector by this column forms the corresponding hidden activation before its nonlinearity.

steps.title: Repeat the dense pattern
steps.description: The next matrix maps hidden activations to output activations. Dense connectivity means arithmetic and weight storage grow with both adjacent layer widths.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Spatial Feature Extraction
question: Where does spatial feature extraction become classification?
scope: Schematic image classifier; the displayed probabilities illustrate the final output, not a measured zebra prediction.

steps.title: Reuse local filters
steps.description: The kernel samples a local patch of the zebra image. Convolution and ReLU create feature maps rather than immediately choosing a class.

steps.title: Transform spatial maps
steps.description: Repeated convolution and pooling stages carry spatial features forward while changing their representation. Pooling and convolution have different roles despite their neighboring positions.

steps.title: Cross the representation boundary
steps.description: Flattening rearranges feature-map entries into a vector consumed by dense layers; it is a layout transformation rather than a learned classifier by itself.

steps.title: Produce class probabilities
steps.description: The final softmax converts classifier scores into the Horse, Zebra, and Dog probability vector.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Convolution Operation
question: Which input values contribute to the highlighted output cell?
scope: Valid 3×3 convolution on a 7×7 input; no numeric filter weights are supplied.

steps.title: Nine neighboring inputs
steps.description: The orange 3×3 patch contains the nine spatial positions used for one output value per input channel.

steps.title: One patch maps to one output
steps.description: The blue guide lines associate this patch with the violet cell in the 5×5 output. The figure depicts dependency, not physical data-transfer paths.

steps.title: Share weights across positions
steps.description: The same learned filter is applied at other valid input positions. This reuse yields translation equivariance without allocating a separate filter for each position.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: im2col Transformation
question: What extra representation does im2col create before matrix multiplication?
scope: Two 3×3 channels and two 2×2 kernels; output multiplication is not drawn.

steps.title: Collect one patch from each channel
steps.description: The red outline on the blue channel selects 1, 2, 4, and 5. Each sliding-window position also includes four entries from the orange channel.

steps.title: Store patches as rows
steps.description: The 4×8 matrix contains one row per window position and eight columns for the two channels. Overlapping input positions appear in multiple rows, increasing temporary storage.

steps.title: Align the kernel vector
steps.description: The two 2×2 kernels become one 8×1 column. Multiplying the lowered matrix by this column produces four output positions, although the product is not shown.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Residual Connection Block (Original Post-Activation Form)
question: What exactly bypasses the weight layers in this residual block?
scope: Original post-activation ResNet form, not a pre-activation block.

steps.title: Compute the residual branch
steps.description: The main branch applies a weight layer, ReLU, and a second weight layer to form F(x).

steps.title: Retain the original input
steps.description: The upper path carries x around both weight layers without those transformations. The addition combines F(x) with this retained input.

steps.title: Apply the final activation
steps.description: The bottom ReLU acts after addition, so the block output is ReLU(F(x)+x). The post-addition nonlinearity matters when reasoning about gradients.

title: Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding
question: Why does a longer RNN sequence reuse parameters but add sequential work?
scope: Three unfolded steps illustrate a recurrent cell with shared weights; hidden-state values differ at each time.

steps.title: Read one recurrent cell
steps.description: The compact graph maps input x and previous hidden state through W_hx and W_hh, then maps hidden state to output through W_yh.

steps.title: Follow the hidden-state dependency
steps.description: The horizontal arrow passes h from one time step to the next. The current step requires the preceding state even though input projections can have separate implementation choices.

steps.title: Reuse the same matrices
steps.description: The repeated W labels denote shared parameters, not separate learned matrices for each time step. Sequence length adds activations and work without increasing these parameter matrices.

title: Illustrative Attention Pattern
question: What does the illustrated attention from “they” reveal—and what does it not prove?
scope: Hypothetical attention strengths, not measured weights or a causal explanation of model behavior.

steps.title: Choose the query position
steps.description: The violet “they” token is the position whose attention links are illustrated. Every line originates at this same query position.

steps.title: Inspect stronger associations
steps.description: Thicker hypothetical links connect to student, finish, and homework. Thickness encodes the schematic weight magnitude rather than sentence order or execution time.

steps.title: Direct access is not proof of reasoning
steps.description: The links connect distant positions without recurrent hops. This illustrates attention connectivity, but the pattern alone does not establish a faithful explanation of a model decision.

title: Query-Key-Value Attention Mechanism
question: How does one attention matrix connect queries, keys, and values?
scope: Six tokens; cell colors are illustrative, not calculated attention probabilities.

steps.title: Compare a query with every key
steps.description: Each cyan query row meets six red key paths. Six queries by six keys create 36 pairwise comparison entries.

steps.title: Distinguish structure from weights
steps.description: The grid represents the dense attention pattern. Its blue-to-red gradient is an illustration and cannot be read as computed probabilities.

steps.title: Aggregate values for each output
steps.description: Each attention row weights the green values to form one output position. Materializing all dense weights stores a quantity growing quadratically with sequence length.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: QKV Projection Computation
question: How can one projection multiplication produce Q, K, and V?
scope: Only the first token output row is drawn; the declared output has six rows.

steps.title: Start with six embedding rows
steps.description: Each of the six token pieces supplies a 768-element embedding row. The first row drawn is labeled Data.

steps.title: Pack three projections side by side
steps.description: The weight matrix has 2304 output columns: 768 each for queries, keys, and values. The color blocks preserve their separate identities within one multiplication.

steps.title: Add bias and retain all token positions
steps.description: A bias vector is added to each projected row. The displayed QKV row is only the first of the six rows in the result; packing does not discard the other tokens.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)
question: Which connections distinguish the transformer decoder from the encoder?
scope: Original encoder–decoder architecture; not a decoder-only model diagram.

steps.title: Supply order information
steps.description: Positional encodings are added to token embeddings before the stacks. Attention without positional information does not encode sequence order by itself.

steps.title: Encode all input positions
steps.description: The left stack alternates attention and feed-forward transformations, each with residual and normalization paths. The repetition bracket denotes repeated layers.

steps.title: Preserve decoder causality
steps.description: Masked self-attention restricts access to future output positions. The next attention block also receives the encoder representations through the cross-stack connection.

steps.title: Predict the output token
steps.description: The decoder feeds a linear projection and softmax. Parallel training across known positions does not eliminate autoregressive dependencies during generation.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Prefill and Decode
question: Why do prompt processing and token generation stress different resources?
scope: Schematic small-batch autoregressive inference; compute/bandwidth classifications are typical regimes, not timing measurements.

steps.title: Process the prompt together
steps.description: Prefill applies matrix–matrix products over all prompt positions, reusing each model weight across those tokens.

steps.title: Keep keys and values
steps.description: Prefill writes the prompt keys and values to the KV cache. This persistent per-request state remains available for later token generation.

steps.title: Read history and append one entry
steps.description: Each decode output becomes the next input. Every step reads the existing cache and adds one token’s keys and values, while rereading model weights.

steps.title: Relate reuse to the bottleneck
steps.description: Prompt-wide weight reuse often makes prefill compute-bound. At small batch, repeatedly reading weights and cache often makes decode bandwidth-bound.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Three Memory Regimes of a Long Context
question: Which memory term dominates as context length increases?
scope: GPT-2 XL shape in FP16 beyond its trained context; scores are for one materialized layer, cache for one request, not total training memory.

steps.title: Separate the allocations
steps.description: The blue weights remain fixed; the orange request cache grows linearly; the red dashed single-layer score matrix grows quadratically. These are different objects and lifetimes.

steps.title: Cache can exceed the model weights
steps.description: Near the labeled 10K-token crossing, the persistent cache for one request becomes larger than the FP16 weights.

steps.title: Avoid materializing quadratic scores
steps.description: The red score curve reaches the device-memory line near 41K tokens. Tiled attention avoids storing this full matrix; it does not remove the need for per-request KV state.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: DLRM Pipeline
question: Why can recommendation combine compute-heavy and memory-heavy stages?
scope: Schematic DLRM pipeline; embedding-table capacity and placement depend on workload.

steps.title: Transform dense features
steps.description: Age and time-of-day features pass through the bottom MLP. Its small weight matrices support dense arithmetic.

steps.title: Gather rather than multiply a table
steps.description: Each categorical ID selects one embedding row. These random reads perform little arithmetic and may require tables larger than one device’s memory.

steps.title: Combine feature representations
steps.description: Pairwise dot products combine the dense representation with gathered embedding vectors. The top MLP maps the interaction result to click probability.

title: Data Movement Primitives
question: When does data movement copy, partition, collect, or combine values?
scope: Four schematic primitives; arrow positions do not encode latency or bandwidth.

steps.title: Broadcast replicates; scatter partitions
steps.description: Broadcast sends the same red value to every destination. Scatter sends different elements from a collection to different destinations.

steps.title: Gather preserves separate elements
steps.description: The bottom-left destination receives the red, yellow, green, and blue entries together. Collecting does not imply performing arithmetic on their values.

steps.title: Reduction combines values
steps.description: The bottom-right primitive sums 1, 3, 5, and 7 into 16. The result is an aggregate rather than the original list.

title: Architecture Selection Decision Framework
question: Why is a plausible architecture only the start of system design?
scope: Decision framework for dense architecture candidates; sparse high-cardinality recommendation is handled separately in the text.

steps.title: Choose an initial structural match
steps.description: Text, temporal sequences, images, and tabular data suggest different candidate families. These branches propose starting points rather than proving a best model.

steps.title: Check resource feasibility
steps.description: A candidate must fit memory and computation budgets and meet inference speed requirements. Failure sends the design toward scaling down or changing architecture.

steps.title: Check quality and deployment together
steps.description: An accuracy miss can require more capacity, while hardware incompatibility can require another design. Follow the return paths to reconsider the candidate after each change.

title: An Example Data Selection Pipeline
question: Where can a data intervention enter the training process?
scope: One possible combination of interventions; the arrows do not require synthetic generation to occur only after dynamic selection.

steps.title: Pay for static selection before training
steps.description: Static pruning removes or retains samples before the target training run. Its scoring work belongs in the intervention cost.

steps.title: Separate selection timing from generation
steps.description: Dynamic selection changes which samples training consumes. Synthetic generation creates candidate data on demand and can also enter independently or feed later selection.

steps.title: Evaluate net data value
steps.description: The ICR evaluation asks whether quality gains justify compute costs. A visually smaller dataset does not by itself establish a cheaper or better training result.

title: Illustrative Compute-Optimal Frontier
question: Why can two systems below a frontier require different interventions?
scope: Conceptual normalized-compute illustration, not a fitted Chinchilla result or a guaranteed intervention trajectory.

steps.title: Read the same budget correctly
steps.description: At a given horizontal compute coordinate, height denotes model performance. The green curve represents a conceptual best allocation rather than measured universal limits.

steps.title: Distinguish a compute constraint
steps.description: The red compute-starved point is paired with a more-training arrow that moves both right and up. This intervention spends more compute rather than claiming free quality.

steps.title: Distinguish a data constraint
steps.description: The orange better-selection arrow rises at the same plotted compute coordinate. It illustrates reallocating a fixed budget toward more useful data, not a guarantee that selection reaches the frontier.

title: Illustrative Diminishing Returns of Data
question: How do equal data budget and equal quality give different comparisons?
scope: Synthetic diminishing-return curves; real workloads need not share their shape or plateau.

steps.title: Hold dataset size fixed
steps.description: The red vertical arrow compares the two curves at one dataset size. Its height is a quality gap at equal data budget.

steps.title: Hold quality fixed instead
steps.description: A horizontal comparison asks how much data each curve needs for the same quality. The more rapidly rising blue curve reaches many intermediate targets sooner.

steps.title: Do not extrapolate the example
steps.description: Both synthetic curves approach the same plotted plateau. The picture motivates measuring data value; it does not prove every selection method improves every dataset.

title: The Selection Inequality
question: When does selection save end-to-end training time?
scope: Normalized illustrative costs at matched quality; savings include selection overhead, not just subset training.

steps.title: Establish the full-training baseline
steps.description: The blue baseline costs 100 normalized time units. It is the total against which a selected-subset pipeline must be compared.

steps.title: Include cheap selection in the total
steps.description: Efficient selection costs 5 and subset training costs 40, totaling 45. The net saving is 55 relative to 100, rather than the 60 suggested by subset training alone.

steps.title: Expensive scoring can erase the gain
steps.description: The expensive selector costs 60 before the same 40-unit subset training. Its total is 100, so reducing training samples produces no net time saving here.

title: Illustrative Boundary-Focused Selection
question: What changes when the selection budget stays fixed at five samples?
scope: Illustrative boundary-focused selection; not a guarantee of representative coverage or final accuracy.

steps.title: Count the same sample budget
steps.description: The orange outlines in the left panel mark five random selections. Their distribution spreads the budget across the feature space.

steps.title: Spend the budget near the boundary
steps.description: The green outlines in the right panel mark five selected samples concentrated near the current boundary. The yellow band identifies the uncertain region being prioritized.

steps.title: Retain the coverage question
steps.description: Boundary focus can target uncertain decisions, but may neglect other regions. Its benefit must justify the scoring work and be checked on appropriate evaluation data.

title: The Active Learning Closed Loop
question: How does active learning turn scoring work into new labels?
scope: Pool-based selection cycle; oracle labels and model updates are not assumed error-free.

steps.title: Score candidates before querying
steps.description: The unlabeled pool feeds a selection strategy. Uncertainty, diversity, or coverage criteria choose which annotation requests are worth making.

steps.title: Acquire labels from the oracle
steps.description: Selected queries go to the human oracle; returned labels join the training set. Choosing a sample and obtaining its label are distinct operations.

steps.title: Close the loop with a new model
steps.description: Training updates the model, whose new state changes subsequent selection. Scoring and retraining consume compute even when they reduce annotation demand.

title: The Active Learning Multiplier
question: How is the illustrated fourfold label-efficiency gap read?
scope: Illustrative accuracy curves, not a measured guarantee for active learning.

steps.title: Fix a target accuracy
steps.description: Near 90 percent accuracy, compare where each curve reaches the same vertical level. Comparing arbitrary endpoints would mix label budget and quality.

steps.title: Read multiplicative label counts
steps.description: The horizontal sample axis is logarithmic. The arrow illustrates reaching similar accuracy with roughly one quarter as many labeled samples, rather than four percentage points more accuracy.

steps.title: Account for the other work
steps.description: The plot compares annotation demand. Selection scoring, model updates, and the reliability of the oracle still determine whether the full active-learning loop is worthwhile.

title: The Domain Gap Problem
question: Why does matching synthetic and real feature coverage require validation?
scope: Schematic marginal densities; they do not determine class-conditional boundaries or establish a causal quality effect.

steps.title: Locate the feature shift
steps.description: The blue synthetic density is shifted left of the orange real density. Their overlap and mismatch describe feature coverage, not classifier accuracy directly.

steps.title: Separate densities from boundaries
steps.description: The dashed red and dotted green lines are schematic decision boundaries drawn with the distributions. Marginal densities alone cannot establish where class boundaries belong.

steps.title: Evaluate on the deployment domain
steps.description: Synthetic data can expand supply while preserving a domain gap. Real-domain validation and class-conditional evidence are needed before treating more generated examples as more useful training signal.

title: Cost Amortization in Foundation Models
question: When does a shared pretraining cost pay off across tasks?
scope: Illustrative compute-only GPU-hour accounting; costs exclude deployment quality and other project expenses.

steps.title: Repeat the scratch-training bill
steps.description: Each task on the left pays its own training-from-scratch cost. The equal-height bars accumulate linearly with the number of tasks.

steps.title: Pay a large fixed cost once
steps.description: The foundation-model strategy pays pretraining up front, then adds much smaller fine-tuning costs per task. A low marginal cost is different from a low total at the start.

steps.title: Check the snapshot before declaring savings
steps.description: The ten-task totals are comparable and the foundation approach remains slightly more expensive at this snapshot. More reuse can cross the compute-only break-even point; the shared model must still meet task quality requirements.

title: ResNet-50 Data Path on One H100
question: Which stage does a data-selection technique actually relieve?
scope: One ImageNet epoch on the chapter’s modeled ResNet-50/H100 path; loads are per full epoch at the compute-bound rate.

steps.title: Trace all four stages
steps.description: Images are read from storage, decoded and augmented on the host, transferred over PCIe, then processed on the accelerator. Cutting arithmetic does not automatically cut every preceding stage.

steps.title: Distinguish materialization from discard
steps.description: A materialized coreset avoids reading excluded images; stream-and-discard filtering still reads them. Both may reduce training arithmetic while leaving different storage and host loads.

steps.title: Account for added artifacts and scoring
steps.description: Offline distillation logits add data to the path, and a scoring pass adds forward arithmetic. The red host outline emphasizes that decoding and augmentation must keep pace with the accelerator.

review_notes: Inspected freshly rebuilt canonical artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json on white; original geometry, printed labels, and plot qualifications retained.

title: Distributed Coreset Selection Architecture
question: What must a coordinator do after workers score separate data shards?
scope: Processes are on one host and workers drive accelerators; coordination must cost less than the training it saves.

steps.title: Score independent shards
steps.description: Worker 0, Worker 1, and Worker N perform local EL2N scoring over their assigned images. Parallel local work reduces what any one worker must score.

steps.title: Merge a global selection
steps.description: Upward arrows deliver local scoring results to the coordinator. A global merge still requires work and host-memory capacity; local scores alone do not define a consistent final subset.

steps.title: Return the selected indices
steps.description: Downward arrows distribute the final coreset indices to workers. The architecture is useful only if scoring and coordination overhead remain below the training time saved.

review_notes: Corrected canonical chapter artwork inspected: coordinator labels now collect shard-local EL2N scores, merge and rerank local selections, and broadcast final indices. Source art, alt text, and local prose agree; worker and arrow geometry is retained.

title: Data Selection Decision Tree
question: How does the binding data problem narrow candidate techniques?
scope: Decision aid rather than a unique optimal policy; multiple constraints can require multiple branches.

steps.title: Start with the binding constraint
steps.description: The top question distinguishes expensive labeling, expensive compute, and insufficient data. A technique chosen without this diagnosis may optimize the wrong resource.

steps.title: Use the available supervision
steps.description: The labeling branch asks about a large pool and an oracle. Those conditions separate self-supervised, semi-supervised, and active-learning candidates.

steps.title: Use redundancy and data sources
steps.description: The compute branch separates redundancy reduction from curriculum choices. The scarcity branch distinguishes a teacher, simulator, or augmentation route. These leaves identify candidates that still need evaluation.

title: The Optimization Stack
question: Which artifacts change as an optimization travels toward deployment?
scope: Artifact-flow schematic; less training data does not imply smaller model weights or cheaper serving.

steps.title: Change the training input first
steps.description: Raw data passes through selection into a curated artifact. This intervention changes what training consumes and can change quality as well as cost.

steps.title: Separate data savings from model compression
steps.description: Training emits a model; compression produces a compact model later. Reducing examples upstream does not automatically reduce the resulting parameter count.

steps.title: Measure the deployment consequence
steps.description: Hardware executes the compact model to form a deployed system. Quality, latency, and resource effects must be checked across these artifact boundaries rather than inferred from one smaller dataset.

title: The Inference Pipeline
question: Why is model execution only part of inference latency?
scope: A stage schematic, without timing encoded by icon spacing or arrow length.

post.label: Raw output postprocessing and final output

steps.title: Prepare a model-ready input
steps.description: Preprocessing transforms raw data into the representation expected by the neural network. Its work occurs before model arithmetic can consume the input.

steps.title: Execute the model
steps.description: The neural network converts prepared input into raw model output. This stage can dominate some workloads, but the diagram deliberately retains the surrounding operations.

steps.title: Return a usable result
steps.description: Postprocessing converts raw outputs into the final response. End-to-end latency must include this stage as well as preprocessing and inference.

title: Inference Server Anatomy
question: How does a server decouple irregular requests from accelerator execution?
scope: Logical server stages; no queue capacity, batch window, service duration, or throughput is encoded by the arrows.

steps.title: Admit requests separately from executing them
steps.description: Network ingress handles arriving client requests before accelerator work begins. This separates network-facing work from the device execution path.

steps.title: Distinguish waiting from batch formation
steps.description: The queue absorbs waiting requests; the dynamic batcher groups work for efficient execution. Waiting may improve utilization while consuming the response-time budget.

steps.title: Dispatch through a runner
steps.description: The inference runner prepares executable work for the accelerator. Optimizing the runner and hardware does not erase ingress, queue, or batching delay.

title: One Request on One Node
question: How much of one request is actually spent on the accelerator?
scope: Reference single ResNet-50 request; network, serialization, and batching delay are excluded.

idle.label: Accelerator idle while input is prepared

steps.title: Prepare the input on the host
steps.description: JPEG decoding, resizing, and normalization occupy the CPU before the device can run. The GPU remains idle during this preparation interval.

steps.title: Transfer before compute
steps.description: The input crosses PCIe after host preparation. The ResNet-50 forward pass begins only after that dependent copy completes.

steps.title: Finish the request beyond the GPU bar
steps.description: Softmax and top-5 selection return to the host. Accelerator busy time is therefore only part of the request’s displayed latency budget.

title: Request Pipelining
question: How can pipelining improve utilization without changing a model?
scope: Schematic independent CPU and GPU operations; overlap improves steady-state throughput, not necessarily a single request’s intrinsic latency.

steps.title: Find the serial idle interval
steps.description: In row A, preprocessing and GPU execution do not overlap across requests. The accelerator waits again before the next prepared request becomes available.

steps.title: Overlap independent requests
steps.description: In row B, CPU Pre 2 runs while GPU 1 executes. These operations belong to different requests and can use distinct resources concurrently.

steps.title: Read the filled pipeline
steps.description: After the initial fill, the device receives successive ready requests with less idle time. The gain comes from scheduling and resource overlap rather than reducing the model’s arithmetic.

title: The Tail Latency Explosion
question: Why does high average utilization threaten the tail-latency budget?
scope: Illustrative M/M/1 queue with normalized service time; p99 approximation is about 4.6 times mean. The 70 percent marker is not a universal threshold.

steps.title: Read latency relative to service time
steps.description: The vertical axis normalizes delay to service time. Even before saturation, queueing adds latency beyond the time required to serve one request.

steps.title: Reserve headroom before the steep rise
steps.description: The labeled knee is a planning marker, not a model-derived discontinuity. The red curve rises continuously as utilization increases.

steps.title: Protect the tail separately from the mean
steps.description: Near saturation, the p99 curve becomes large before the mean looks equally dramatic. Under the stated queue model, p99 is approximately 4.6 times the mean; real arrival and service patterns require measurement.

title: The Throughput-Latency Knee
question: What does a larger batch buy and what does it cost in this serving model?
scope: Modeled reference profile, not measured benchmarks; one worker waits a 10 ms formation window before serving each batch.

steps.title: Amortize fixed overhead
steps.description: At small batch sizes, more requests share fixed work and the formation window. Throughput rises while latency grows relatively slowly.

steps.title: Read both metrics at the knee
steps.description: The planning knee marks twice the batch-one latency and half the modeled throughput ceiling. It is a stated planning definition rather than a hardware phase transition.

steps.title: Pay increasing latency for diminishing throughput gain
steps.description: At larger batches, throughput approaches its ceiling while latency rises. Each throughput point is batch size divided by the plotted formation-plus-service latency for this single worker.

title: Framework Interoperability
question: What must be compatible on both sides of an ONNX artifact?
scope: Historical framework interoperability schematic; logos do not guarantee current exporter, operator, or runtime support.

steps.title: Export a model representation
steps.description: Inward spokes carry models from source frameworks into ONNX. Export must represent the operations and relevant semantics used by the model.

steps.title: Keep the artifact boundary explicit
steps.description: The central ONNX label denotes a shared representation, not an execution device or an automatic optimizer. A serialized graph still needs compatible consumers.

steps.title: Check the destination support
steps.description: Outward spokes denote loading into tools or runtimes. Successful portability requires operator and semantic support at both export and load boundaries.

title: The KV-Cache Explosion
question: Why do context length and concurrency compete for the same memory?
scope: FP16 KV cache for a 70B-class GQA model after INT4 weights; budget is before runtime overhead and chart rounds it to 51 GB.

steps.title: Subtract persistent weights first
steps.description: The dashed red line is the remaining cache budget after model weights, not the entire accelerator capacity. Runtime workspace can reduce the usable remainder further.

steps.title: Grow all concurrent request caches
steps.description: Each curve rises with context length, and its slope increases with batch size. Batch 32 reaches the budget near 4.8K tokens because 32 request caches draw from the same remaining HBM.

steps.title: Trade context for concurrency
steps.description: Batch 16 can sustain longer contexts before reaching the same budget; batches 1 and 4 use less cache at a given context. Allocation schemes can reduce waste but cannot remove these required KV entries.

title: Intelligence Deflation
question: What does a historical API price floor show about serving economics?
scope: Dated input-token list prices for named versions; not current quotes, equivalent-quality measurements, or full operating costs.

steps.title: Read the dated unit
steps.description: The vertical axis gives dollars per one million input tokens on a log scale. Each point belongs to a model version and announcement date.

steps.title: Distinguish a floor from every model price
steps.description: Later models show a wide range of prices. The fit uses successive new lows, so a non-floor point such as DeepSeek-V3 need not lie on it.

steps.title: Limit the economic inference
steps.description: The falling historical floor motivates new workflow economics. It does not compare equal quality or account for output tokens, cache policies, and a complete deployed service.

title: The Responsible Engineering Lifecycle
question: How do responsible-engineering requirements become continuing operational work?
scope: Lifecycle and resource-accounting schematic; controls supply evidence rather than automatic legal compliance.

steps.title: Turn goals into release evidence
steps.description: Specify names the target populations and oversight boundary. Measure evaluates those requirements per slice and can require mitigation training.

steps.title: Carry explanation and monitoring into production
steps.description: Explain and document makes decisions and models reviewable; Operate collects per-group telemetry. Operational evidence feeds the next specification rather than ending at release.

steps.title: Budget and govern the entire lifecycle
steps.description: Resource and Govern span all four stages. Labeled data, reviewer hours, explanation compute, telemetry, energy, and audit evidence remain engineering costs across the lifecycle.

title: Threshold Effects on Subgroup Outcomes
question: How can aggregate accuracy improve while one subgroup receives worse outcomes?
scope: Sixteen illustrative cases; approve markers to the left of a boundary. Boundary labels show achieved accuracy, not score cutoff.

steps.title: Decode the markers before classifying
steps.description: Circles denote loan repayment and plus signs default; color identifies subgroup. Approval is determined by position to the left of the selected boundary.

steps.title: Apply the75 percent boundary
steps.description: At the left boundary, count approved and rejected markers against their true outcomes. Overall accuracy alone hides which subgroup contributes each error.

steps.title: Inspect who receives the accuracy gain
steps.description: Moving to the right boundary perfectly separates Subgroup A. Subgroup B’s errors rise from one to three even as aggregate accuracy reaches 81.25 percent, so the aggregate gain does not establish subgroup improvement.

title: An Illustrative Fairness-Accuracy Pareto Frontier
question: How should the three operating points on this fairness frontier be compared?
scope: Hypothetical demographic-disparity frontier with inverted horizontal axis; no universal or empirical trade-off is claimed.

steps.title: Read the axis direction
steps.description: Disparity decreases toward the right. Point A has the highest plotted accuracy and larger demographic disparity than B and C.

steps.title: Interpret the stated ratio narrowly
steps.description: B’s disparity 0.05 is 3.6 times smaller than A’s 0.18. The label does not define a universal multiplier for fairness or a causal effect of one intervention.

steps.title: Identify the assumed cost of equality
steps.description: Point C has zero disparity and lower accuracy on this constructed curve. The example illustrates an operating choice rather than proving that real systems must sacrifice this much accuracy.

title: Model Interpretability Spectrum
question: What kind of evidence is needed to audit different model families?
scope: Schematic grouping; interpretability depends on model size and feature meaning, not just family name.

steps.title: Inspect model logic when it is tractable
steps.description: Decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression occupy the intrinsic group. Direct inspection still depends on manageable size and meaningful input features.

steps.title: Validate a separate explanation
steps.description: Random forests, neural networks, and CNN/transformer models are grouped as requiring post-hoc explanation here. Methods such as LIME or SHAP introduce a fidelity question rather than exposing the complete model directly.

steps.title: Avoid treating the spectrum as quality ranking
steps.description: The continuum frames an auditability trade-off. A farther-right model is not automatically more accurate, less safe, or impossible to understand in every application.

title: Cost of Training Notable Models
question: What do estimated frontier-training costs say about access to large training runs?
scope: Historical final-run compute costs in constant 2023 dollars, not full research budgets, current hardware quotes, or inference expense.

steps.title: Separate frontier and notable runs
steps.description: Red points are models flagged as frontier at release; gray points are other notable models. Both are estimated training-run costs, not every expense of producing a model.

steps.title: Read constant-dollar log costs
steps.description: The vertical log axis represents multiplicative differences in constant 2023 US dollars. Recent frontier estimates extend into the highest plotted cost region.

steps.title: Restrict the fitted trend to its evidence
steps.description: The dashed fit is calculated over frontier points. It summarizes these historical estimates and motivates access constraints without forecasting the cost of every future model.

title: Data Governance Framework
question: Why does governance require both organizational and technical elements?
scope: Eight-element operating framework; circular placement denotes coordination rather than a required execution order.

steps.title: Assign authority and responsibilities
steps.description: Organization and policies establish ownership and rules for handling data. A technical control without a responsible operating process cannot complete this governance role.

steps.title: Make data meaning and provenance inspectable
steps.description: Sourcing, catalogs, shared definitions, and quality records establish what data is available, where it came from, and how teams interpret it.

steps.title: Operate and secure the governed lifecycle
steps.description: Data operations and security enact those decisions in running systems. These elements coordinate with the others; encryption or documentation alone does not establish compliance.

title: Responsible AI Governance Layers
question: How do external requirements reach the team that builds a system?
scope: Nested oversight model, not a certification checklist or automatic proof of compliance.

steps.title: Identify the outer requirements
steps.description: Government regulation establishes applicable duties; industry certification and review provide additional oversight structures. Their applicability depends on the system and setting.

steps.title: Translate oversight into operating practice
steps.description: The organization supplies safety culture, design, leadership commitment, training, and review. These structures connect external requirements with engineering work.

steps.title: Build auditable technical evidence
steps.description: At the team center, audit trails, verification and bias testing, explainable interfaces, and software-engineering workflows supply inspectable practices. The inward requirements do not become satisfied merely because a control is named.

title: Advertised GPU Peak Capability Across Generations
question: Why is the advertised GPU peak curve not a same-precision speedup curve?
scope: Single-chip advertised paths mix floating-point and integer operations, precision, and structured-sparsity assumptions; no sustained application performance claim.

sparse.label: A100 H100 and B200 sparse paths

steps.title: Start with the FP32 baseline
steps.description: K20X and M40 labels report FP32 throughput. Their points can be interpreted only together with the operation and precision labels.

steps.title: Notice the quantity changes
steps.description: P40 uses INT8 operations while V100 reports FP16 floating-point throughput. Connecting these points does not make them one consistent same-precision measurement series.

steps.title: Keep sparsity assumptions explicit
steps.description: A100, H100, and B200 labels assume structured sparsity and include narrower numerical formats. The steep advertised curve therefore combines several changes and cannot predict a general application speedup.
